The Rebbe’s mechiras chametz document. (It's one of the only times when the Rebbe signed his name with “ben Harav Levi Yitzchak.")

When the Alter Rebbe first returned home after studying with the Mezritcher Maggid in the year תקכ”ה )1765(, he wanted to do the mitzvah of bedikas chametz with as much kavana as possible. He was so busy preparing that he didn’t even eat the whole day. And, when it was finally time to do the mitzvah, the Alter Rebbe spent the entire night searching for chametz, even though he had just one small room!

There’s an important mitzvah that we do on the night before Erev Pesach. This mitzvah is so important that we aren’t allowed to let anything distract us—not even limmud Torah! Do you know what this mitzvah is? That’s right: ּבְדִיקַת חָמֵץ—searching for chametz.

But, after spending so much time and effort cleaning the house, there might not be any chametz to be found! That’s totally fine, because the mitzvah is just to look for chametz. We don’t have to actually find chametz.

Still, our minhag is to purposefully hide chametz around the house so that we will find some when we search. We hide ten small pieces, making sure that they’re wrapped carefully so no crumbs fall out.

During bedikas chametz, we look around the house with a candle (beeswax is best), a feather, and wooden spoon. Once all of the pieces have been found, we tie the supplies together in a bag (to be burned with the chametz the next morning), and we say “ּכָל חֲמִירָא” to nullify any remaining chametz..

As you surely know, one of the main mitzvos of Pesach is to not own any chametz. But that doesn’t mean we have to throw it all out before Yom Tov!

The Shulchan Aruch says that we can do what’s called מְכִירַת חָמֵץ: We put our chametz into a place where it won’t be seen or touched throughout Pesach and then sell it all to a non- Jew. This way, the chametz doesn’t belong to us anymore, and it can stay in our homes.

There are different ways to do mechiras chametz. The Alter Rebbe says that the best way is to use a method known as “קַּבְּלָן עָרֵב—a guarantor or ‘backup’ person” who takes responsibility for the sale if something goes wrong with the seller. Having an areiv kablan shows that mechiras chametz is a serious sale; we don’t chas v’shalom want to be left owning chametz on Pesach! To make sure that everything is done properly, we first give all of our chametz to the rav, and then he sells it to a non-Jew.

On the morning of Erev Pesach, we do another special mitzvah called “חָמֵץ ּבִיעּור—burning the chametz.” We take the chametz from the night before and burn it in a fire. As it burns, we say Kol Chamira again, plus a special Yehi Ratzon that Hashem should get rid of our Yetzer Hara just as we are getting rid of the chametz. Chametz

A Chassid who spent Pesach of תרע”ד )1914(in Lubavitch with the Rebbe Rashab described bi’ur chametz:

The Rebbe [Rashab] burned his chametz in the furnace of Tomchei Temimim’s zal (study hall). The fire was started very early in the morning so that the flames would be scorching hot by the time bi’ur chametz took place.

When he finished burning the chametz, the Rebbe [Rashab] turned to the temimim and said, “Just like we burned the gashmiyus’dik chametz, we must also burn our ruchniyus’dik chametz.”

The chachamim established a certain fast day that’s only for a specific type of Yid. Do you know which one? It’s the fast called “ּבְכֹורִים ּתַעֲנִית,” and it’s just for bechorim—firstborn men or boys. As we know from the story of Yetzi’as Mitzrayim, Hashem saved the Yiddishe bechorim during Makas Bechoros. To remember this neis, bechorim fast on Erev Pesach. If a bechor is under bar mitzvah, his father fasts for him.

However, the minhag is actually for bechorim not to fast—instead, they try to participate in a siyum on Erev Pesach. This way, they can eat at the siyum’s seudas mitzvah and throughout the rest of the day.

Pesach is a Yom Tov that is packed with mitzvos! For us chayolim, it is also packed with Chabad minhagim. We have special ways to sell chametz, search for chametz,

and burn chametz; our own way to set up the Seder plate; and minhagim for almost every step of the Seder.

Do you like asking questions? I hope so. Questions are so important for learning!

The Seder is full of questions. Even the חָכָם ּבֶן, the wisest of the Four Sons, has questions. The Rebbe tells us that this teaches us a big lesson: That we must ask, ask, ask!

We are soldiers in Hashem’s Army, and we have Kabbalas Ol to do everything that Hashem tells us— whether we understand it or not. But, once we’ve committed to following Hashem’s command no matter what, we are also supposed to understand the reasons for the mitzvos. This helps us to have more chayus when we do them!

So, on the Seder Night and throughout the whole year, always ask questions. Ask why we do the mitzvos and ask about each of their reasons. Ask about our minhagim and our Chassidishe ways. Ask away until you really understand. Ask until every single mission is done with true chayus and bren!
